questions.q: What is the role of redirect_uri in the OAuth authorization code flow?
o: It lists the scopes the client application is asking the user for
It tells the authorization server where to send the code after consent
It is the URL used later to fetch the user's profile from the API
It names which resource server should receive the final access token
questions.x: After approval, the authorization server redirects the browser to redirect_uri with the code. If that URI can be attacker-controlled, the code is delivered to the attacker.
questions.h: The parameter names the destination after approval. What happens if an attacker chooses that destination?

questions.q: What is an OAuth authorization code used for in this flow?
o: It is sent as a Bearer token directly to the resource server API
It is a short-lived value exchanged for an access token after redirect
It is a signed JWT that already encodes every granted user permission
It is a one-time password delivered to the user's phone by SMS
questions.x: The code is short-lived and meant to be single-use. The client (here the blog's oauth-callback) exchanges it for an access token, then establishes the user session.
questions.h: The code is not the final API credential. What does the application do with it after the redirect?

questions.q: What misconfiguration does this lab's OAuth provider have?
o: It uses the implicit flow, putting the access token in the URL hash
It accepts any redirect_uri instead of matching a registered allowlist
It issues access tokens that never expire and cannot be revoked
It embeds the client secret in client-side JavaScript on the blog
questions.x: A correct provider compares redirect_uri to the URIs registered for that client. This provider accepted the exploit-server URL with no error, which is the core bug.
questions.h: The fix is to check redirect_uri. What check is missing when an arbitrary destination is accepted?

questions.q: How does the attacker make the admin send a code to the exploit server?
o: A CSRF form that auto-posts a token-exchange request as the admin user
An exploit-server iframe starts OAuth with the attacker's redirect_uri
An XSS payload injected into the OAuth provider's own login form page
A DNS rebinding trick against the blog's legitimate callback hostname
questions.x: The exploit page loads an iframe pointing at the OAuth authorize URL with redirect_uri set to the exploit server. The admin opens it while already logged in to OAuth.
questions.h: The admin will open anything hosted on the exploit server. What embedded request starts OAuth with a tampered redirect_uri?

questions.q: Why does the admin complete the attacker's OAuth request with no prompt?
o: Admin accounts skip OAuth consent screens by a special role flag
The admin already has an active OAuth session, so the flow auto-completes
The exploit page draws a fake Approve button that the admin must click
The lab provider enables auto-approval for every client, even first use
questions.x: The lab states the admin always has an active session with the OAuth service. Loading the iframe finishes authorization without a login or consent screen, then redirects with the code.
questions.h: The admin is already logged in to the OAuth service. Does a second authorize request still show login and consent?

questions.q: After the code appears in the exploit-server log, what does the attacker do?
o: Send the code as a Bearer token straight to /admin on the blog
Replay the code to the blog's oauth-callback to obtain an admin session
Decode the code as a JWT and copy the admin session claims locally
Save the code as a refresh token and reuse it days later at will
questions.x: The writeup GETs /oauth-callback?code= on the blog with the stolen value. The application completes the exchange and sets an admin session, which is then used to delete carlos.
questions.h: The stolen value is an authorization code, not a session yet. Which blog endpoint is meant to receive that code?

questions.q: Which of the following is true of this lab's redirect_uri hijack?
o: The provider accepts any redirect_uri, including the exploit server
The admin's active OAuth session completes the flow without a prompt
All of these statements are true about this OAuth hijack lab attack
The stolen code is sent to the blog oauth-callback to create a session
questions.x: The provider does not allowlist redirect_uri. The admin's existing OAuth session auto-completes. Replaying the stolen code to oauth-callback yields the admin session used to delete carlos.
questions.h: Check validation of redirect_uri, why the admin sees no prompt, and where the stolen code is replayed.

questions.q: What is the correct fix on the authorization server for this bug?
o: Require HTTPS for redirect_uri but still allow any host or path
Compare redirect_uri with an exact-match allowlist of registered URIs
Add PKCE only, without ever checking the redirect destination
Shrink code lifetime to one second but still accept any redirect_uri
questions.x: Exact-match allowlisting means only URIs registered for that client are accepted. Different paths, subdomains, or hosts must be rejected, not partially matched.
questions.h: The bug is accepting arbitrary destinations. What check only permits URIs that were registered for the client?

questions.q: In this flow, how does the authorization code differ from the access token?
o: They are the same credential, renamed depending on which hop you watch
The code is a short-lived redirect value, the access token is used to call APIs
The access token is placed in the redirect URL, the code stays back-channel
The code is read-only, while the access token is the only way to write data
questions.x: The code travels in the browser redirect and is meant to be short-lived. The access token is obtained in the callback exchange and is what authorizes API calls. Splitting them limits damage if the redirect is stolen, provided redirect_uri is validated.
questions.h: One value is visible in the redirect URL. The other is obtained during callback exchange and used as the API credential. Which is which?

questions.q: What is this lab's goal after the admin OAuth session is hijacked?
o: Change the admin account email to an attacker-controlled inbox
Open /admin with the hijacked session and delete the user carlos
Dump the OAuth client secret from an admin-only settings panel
Send a phishing message to every user from the admin mailbox
questions.x: With the admin session cookie from oauth-callback, the attacker opens /admin and deletes carlos, which is the PortSwigger completion condition for this lab.
questions.h: The admin panel in these labs has a specific target user. Who gets deleted to finish?
